facts.claim: Australian government representatives cannot perform marriage ceremonies and it is not possible to get married at an Australian Embassy or Consulate (Australian Embassy Rome, Marriage in Italy PDF, as at October 2026).

Two main documents are required for Australian citizens to marry in Italy: the Atto Notorio and the Nulla Osta. The Embassy tells couples to contact the marriage office of the city where they intend to marry for the full list of documents for Australian citizens.

The Embassy's information is 'provided for the convenience of enquirers' and neither the Australian Government nor the Embassy takes responsibility for the consequences of using it; revenue stamp costs 'may change without notice'. (Basis for 'as at October 2026' wording and 'your Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements'.)

The Atto Notorio ('Atto di notorietà per uso matrimonio') should be obtained from the Italian Embassy or nearest Italian Consulate in the state where you reside before leaving Australia. If you cannot get it in Australia, it can be obtained from a Tribunale Civile (Civil Court) in Italy or from the civil registrar (ufficiale di stato civile) of the marriage office of the city where you plan to marry.

Tribunale Civile route in Italy: you must call beforehand for an appointment and attend in person with TWO adult witnesses; if either spouse or a witness does not speak Italian an interpreter is needed in addition to the two witnesses; neither spouse can act as witness or interpreter. Payment is by revenue stamps bought in advance: urgent (same day) one EUR 16.00 stamp for the original plus another EUR 16.00 stamp for your copy and three EUR 6.20 stamps; not urgent (collect after 5 days) one EUR 16.00 stamp plus another EUR 16.00 stamp and one EUR 6.20 stamp.
facts.conflicts: Witness count differs by route: 2 at a Tribunale in Italy (Embassy PDF) vs 4 at every Italian consulate in Australia (Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide, Perth). Not a contradiction: different issuing authorities. A competitor claim of 4 witnesses at the comune is not supported by any official source read; the Embassy gives no witness count for the comune route, so the article should not state one.

facts.claim: Italian Consulate General Sydney (NSW residents): the Atto Notorio is signed by the Australian citizen with FOUR witnesses, declaring no impediment under articles 95, 86, 89 and 97 of the Italian Civil Code. The applicants and the 4 witnesses must all be present at the appointment; witnesses must not be related to the bride or groom but can be related to each other; if both partners are Australian each signs their own Atto Notorio and they can use the same witnesses. Book via the Consulate's online 'Services Offered' form (Registry Office, 'Appointment for marriage in Italy') with the Modello 1 details. In Italy it can instead be obtained at any Tribunal.
Italian Consulate General Sydney: the Atto Notorio is valid for six months from the date it is signed, 'therefore it cannot be requested/issued before 6 months from the date of wedding'.

Italian Consulate General Sydney: together with the Atto Notorio, Australian citizens must provide the Italian City Council (comune) with (1) the original birth certificate and an official Italian translation (NAATI), both bearing the Apostille granted by DFAT, and (2) the original Single Status Certificate issued by the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, with an official Italian translation (NAATI), both bearing the DFAT Apostille.

Italian Consulate General Sydney consular tariff (simplified version for the public, fourth quarter 2026): 'Atto Notorio per Matrimonio' EUR 28.00 / AUD 45.70. Payments only by debit card (EFTPOS) or cash in Australian dollars.
facts.conflicts: Date label mismatch: the fees page says the tariff applies 01.11.2026 to 31.12.2026; the PDF header says 1 October to 31 December. Amount is the same; tariffs change quarterly with the exchange rate.

facts.claim: Italian Consulate General Melbourne (Victoria and Tasmania residents): fill in the online application form, book through the Prenot@mi portal, and attend with a current passport, proof of address in Victoria or Tasmania, and 4 adult witnesses with photo ID (passport or driver licence) bearing no relation to the applicants. If one applicant is not an Australian or US citizen, the documents are only needed for the Australian party, but the applicant(s) must always be accompanied by 4 witnesses. If both applicants are also EU citizens, the Atto Notorio is not required. Valid six months from issue.
Italian Consulate General Melbourne: the Atto Notorio costs approximately AUD 45 (depending on the current EUR/AUD exchange rate), payable by debit or credit card.

Italian Consulate Brisbane: Australian citizens present the Atto Notorio to their Embassy or Consulate in Italy to obtain the Nulla Osta, which is then presented to the town hall where the wedding is celebrated. The Atto Notorio is valid for 6 months from issue. Both bride and groom must be present at the appointment along with 4 witnesses (if one partner is not Australian, documents are only required for the Australian). If both applicants are also EU citizens, the Atto Notorio is not required.

Italian Consulate Brisbane fact sheet: contact the Consulate at least one month before your intended departure for Italy. Documents: original full birth certificate with DFAT Apostille and NAATI Italian translation; Letter of No Record of Marriage (QLD residents) or Letter of No Impediment (NT residents) from the BDM Registry with DFAT Apostille and NAATI translation; valid Australian passport; proof of residence; if applicable the Divorce Order (Family Court) with DFAT Apostille and NAATI translation. The couple and 4 witnesses (not family related, who have known the applicant(s) for at least 12 months) attend; allow up to 1 hour. The exact fee is advised after document review and only cash is accepted.

Italian Consulate Adelaide guide (updated 21/06/2021): the Atto Notorio is signed by the future spouses and four witnesses; applicants and witnesses must all be present; spouses can use the same witnesses. Book through the online notarial booking system and provide the required personal details at least two weeks before the appointment. Australians marrying in Italy need the original birth certificate with DFAT Apostille and official Italian translation (NAATI) and a Single Status Certificate (BDM) with DFAT Apostille and official Italian translation.

Italian Consulate Perth (Italian-language page): appointments for the Atto Notorio are requested by email with the request form and copies of passports and WA driver licences for the couple and witnesses. At the appointment: four witnesses (not relatives of the couple and not sharing their surname), each with passport and WA driver licence; the couple's valid passports and WA driver licences; for each Australian partner an original, recently issued birth certificate (multilingual form or with official Italian translation) consistent with the passport; a copy of the divorce order if divorced. Valid 6 months from issue; cost per the consular tariff. The Consulate recommends contacting the comune or church well in advance.

Comune di Montespertoli (Tuscany) foreigners' marriage page: an Australian citizen must produce (a) a sworn declaration made before the Australian consul in Italy that there is no impediment under Australian law, with the consul's signature legalised at the Prefettura, and (b) an atto di notorietà made before the competent Italian authority (abroad, the Italian consul) with four witnesses.

Nulla Osta: in addition to the Atto Notorio, an Australian citizen marrying in Italy makes a Sworn Declaration (Nulla Osta) at the Australian Embassy in Rome or the Australian Consulate-General in Milan. It states there is no impediment to marriage and must be signed, whether you are single, divorced or widowed, in the presence of an Australian consular officer. Travel with your Australian passport, which must be presented when signing. 'Please set an appointment before attending.'
facts.conflicts: Who attends: the Embassy says the Nulla Osta is signed by each Australian citizen in person before a consular officer and charged 'per Australian citizen'. Whether a non-Australian partner must attend is not published.

facts.claim: 'Nulla Ostas sworn outside of Italy and Certificates of No Impediment are not valid for use in Italy.' (Australian Embassy Rome)
facts.conflicts: Smartraveller's general page lists a DFAT Certificate of No Impediment (CNI) as a common document for marrying overseas and says some authorities only accept locally issued CNIs. For Italy, the Embassy's specific rule (CNI not valid) governs.

facts.claim: If previously married, the consular officer witnessing the Nulla Osta must see the ORIGINAL divorce certificate or death certificate of the late spouse; photocopies are not accepted. All certificates must be originals.

A divorced woman who wishes to marry again within 300 days of her divorce must seek special permission from an Italian magistrate through the local Italian authorities; otherwise 300 days must elapse. (Comune di Montespertoli also states that a divorced or widowed woman free for less than 300 days needs Tribunal authorisation under articles 116 and 89 of the Civil Code.)

The Nulla Osta (Sworn Declaration) is valid for six months and costs the Euro equivalent of A$80.00 per Australian citizen. Payments only by credit or debit card at the Embassy in Rome; cash is not accepted.
facts.conflicts: Validity: 6 months (Embassy, official) vs '3 months, A$70' on a planner site (peachperfectweddings, outdated; not a source) and 'approx 50 AUD' (wowitaly-weddings). Fee: the undated Embassy PDF says the euro equivalent of A$80; the Embassy's notarial services page lists A$88 for 'administering an oath or receiving a declaration' (fee schedule from 1 January 2025); DFAT/Smartraveller's current schedule (from 1 January 2026) lists A$90 for 'administer an affidavit (oath, declaration or affirmation)' delivered overseas. Which figure applies to the Nulla Osta is unconfirmed.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Rome notarial services page: notarial services are offered in person and by appointment only at the Embassy in Rome and the Consulate-General in Milan (not elsewhere in Italy). Bring a valid passport or ID card and original documents. Electronic payment only (no cash), non-refundable. The Embassy and Consulate-General do not provide translations and refer to NAATI for certified translators and interpreters. Listed fees (schedule from 1 January 2025, AUD): receiving a declaration A$88; Apostille A$102; CNI A$177.
facts.conflicts: This page shows the 2025 fee schedule; Smartraveller shows the 2026 schedule (A$90 / A$105 / A$181). Use the 2026 figures if stating any DFAT fee.

facts.claim: DFAT notarial fees (schedule from 1 January 2026, AUD): Document legalisation: Apostille A$105; Authentication certificate A$105; Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage A$181 (in Australia and overseas). Overseas-only services such as administering an affidavit (oath, declaration or affirmation) A$90. Fees rise with CPI on 1 January each year. In Australia payment is by EFTPOS, MasterCard or Visa; cash is not accepted.

DFAT document legalisation: ask the overseas authority which documents it needs legalised; if a document is not an original Australian public document it must first be notarised by an Australian Notary Public; the apostille is applied directly to the document (get a notarised copy legalised if you do not want originals marked, provided the overseas authority accepts it). Lodge at any Australian Passport Office by appointment (someone can attend on your behalf) or by registered mail to the Authentications Section in Melbourne or Sydney; several documents can go on one request form. Processing times vary, with delays at the end of the school year and in peak holiday periods (Smartraveller, last updated 30/09/2026).

Smartraveller (last updated 18/08/2026): BDM registries can issue a statement that there is no record of a previous marriage, a Single Status certificate or a No Record Result certificate; local authorities may also ask for divorce papers, a deceased spouse's death certificate and your original birth certificate and passport. Smartraveller says it cannot tell you what a destination needs and to contact that country's embassy or consulate.

Legalisation: once obtained, the Nulla Osta must be legalised by the Ufficio Legalizzazioni of the Prefettura; any Prefettura in Italy will do (Rome: Via Stendhal 1, open Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday 9:00am to 12:00pm). Before going, buy a revenue stamp (marca da bollo) costing EUR 16.00 at a tobacconist (tabaccaio); the Prefettura official applies it to the Nulla Osta. Stamp costs may change without notice.

Comune di Montespertoli: a Nulla Osta issued by a foreign Embassy or Consulate in Italy must have the consular signature legalised at the Prefettura unless the country is party to a convention exempting it; Australia is not on the comune's exempt list.

Civil ceremony: first take the Atto Notorio and the Nulla Osta to the Ufficio Matrimoni (Marriage Office) of the city where you plan to marry. If you do not speak Italian, bring someone who speaks Italian and can translate. You are given one appointment to lodge your Declaration of Intent to Marry and another for the ceremony; 'these appointments may fall on the same day'. The Declaration of Intent is followed by the civil ceremony. It is customary to pay a fee for the rental of the marriage hall, which varies by location.
facts.conflicts: Timing of the declaration: the Embassy says the declaration and ceremony may fall on the same day; the comuni of Bagno a Ripoli and Montespertoli require the sworn declaration (verbale) at least three days before the wedding. It varies by comune.

facts.claim: If one party is Italian, or is an Australian with Italian residency, the Italian authorities may require banns (pubblicazione di matrimonio) to be posted for at least two weeks before the wedding.

Comune di Bagno a Ripoli (Florence): foreign citizens, whether resident in Italy or abroad, may contract a civil, concordat (Catholic) or religious marriage in an Italian comune. If both partners are foreign and neither is resident or domiciled in Italy, instead of banns they sign a verbale (sworn declaration) of no impediment under articles 85 to 88 of the Civil Code, by appointment, at least three days before the wedding, presenting the nulla osta. The sworn declaration has no cost.

Comune di Bagno a Ripoli: a foreign citizen who does not speak Italian perfectly must be assisted by a translator-interpreter with valid ID both when lodging the request and during the ceremony. The comune does not provide the interpreter; the couple must find one in good time.

Comune di Bagno a Ripoli: the ceremony can take place in the town hall council chamber or at external locations listed by the comune ('Luoghi e tariffe'). Request the date and room at least 90 days before; send the payment receipt and the form naming the witnesses (one per partner) and the choice of foreign law for property relations at least 15 days before. The celebration cost varies by location. After the ceremony the registrar transcribes the marriage in the civil register and issues the marriage certificate or extract (certificato / estratto di matrimonio).

Comune di Montespertoli confirms the same rules for two non-resident foreigners: a verbale of no impediment signed by appointment at least three days before the wedding (instead of banns), and a translator-interpreter at the request and at the ceremony for anyone who does not know Italian perfectly.

Marriage certificate: you may apply for a marriage certificate (certificato di matrimonio) shortly before the ceremony and should receive it immediately after. Ask the Italian authorities at the Prefettura of the city where you marry to affix an Apostille to the Italian marriage certificate 'so that it may [be] legally valid once you return to Australia'. During peak marriage season (May to September) it can be difficult to get an appointment for the marriage celebrant and to apply for the Apostille.

Comune di Parma: multilingual civil status extracts (estratti plurilingue) are issued under the Vienna Convention of 8 September 1976 and are valid among the signatory countries without translation or legalisation; the service is free; there are no multilingual extracts for civil unions.
facts.conflicts: Read via the page summary/extraction, not full text. Whether Australian agencies accept an Italian multilingual extract without translation is not published; the Embassy's advice is an Apostille on the Italian marriage certificate.

facts.claim: Concordat (Catholic) marriage: celebrated before a Catholic minister under the agreements between the Holy See and the Italian State (Lateran Concordat 1929); it has civil effects provided the marriage act is transcribed in the civil registers, after marriage publications at both the parish and the comune. The priest reads articles 143, 144 and 147 of the Civil Code and sends the act to the registrar within 5 days; the registrar transcribes it within 24 hours; the civil effects run from the day of the ceremony.

Marrying in Australia instead: give a Notice of Intended Marriage to an authorised celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the wedding (it can be completed from overseas); be married by an authorised celebrant physically present with 2 witnesses. Overseas marriages cannot be performed by an Australian-authorised celebrant or registered in Australia (Attorney-General's Department).

Smartraveller (last updated 18/08/2026): 'You can't register an overseas marriage in Australia. But in most cases, your marriage is legally recognised here.' To be recognised it must have been valid under the law of the country where it happened and valid under Australian law had it occurred in Australia. A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of the marriage, but you may be unable to use it as proof of a name change; check with your state or territory registry. 'Talk to a lawyer to confirm your overseas marriage certificate is valid in Australia.' Not recognised where a party was already married, not old enough, too closely related, or forced.

Attorney-General's Department: an overseas marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was valid in the overseas country and would have been valid here. You may be able to use your overseas marriage certificate to prove you got married, but some states and territories do not accept overseas marriage certificates for a change of name.

Marriage Act 1961, Part VA (Recognition of foreign marriages), s 88D(1): 'a marriage to which this Part applies shall be recognised in Australia as valid', subject to s 88D(2) exceptions (a party already validly married; where a party was domiciled in Australia, a party not of marriageable age; prohibited relationship; no real consent).
facts.source: https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdb/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ma196185/s88d.html (text of Marriage Act 1961 s 88D; official series https://www.legislation.gov.au/Series/C1961A00012)

facts.claim: NSW Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages (page modified 21/10/2026): overseas marriages cannot be registered in Australia and you cannot be issued an Australian marriage certificate, but the marriage will usually be recognised if legal where it took place and it would be legal in Australia. You need to have registered the marriage in the country where it took place and have evidence such as the marriage certificate. In NSW an overseas marriage certificate cannot be used to change your surname; apply for an official change of name instead (this does not mean the marriage is not recognised).

Births, Deaths and Marriages Victoria (updated 16 October 2024): an overseas marriage cannot be registered in Australia but will generally be recognised; make sure it is registered in the country where it took place and keep evidence. If you were born or married overseas you cannot take your spouse's family name automatically; you need to apply to change your name.

Attorney-General's Department: since 9 December 2017, same-sex marriages that took place overseas are generally recognised in Australia; the Marriage Act defines marriage as 'the union of 2 people to the exclusion of all others, voluntarily entered into for life'. If Australia recognises your marriage you cannot marry again in Australia, but you may hold a confirmation of vows or recommitment ceremony.

Comune di Firenze: Law no. 76 of 20 May 2016 (Legge Cirinnà), in force 5 June 2016, created the civil union (unione civile) as the legal institution for same-sex couples. Two adults of the same sex form a civil union by declaration before the civil registrar in the presence of two witnesses. A foreign citizen must also present a nulla osta from their own country's competent authority; where that is impossible because their country does not recognise same-sex civil unions, it is replaced by a certificate or other document attesting free status, or a substitute declaration under DPR 445/2000. The partners may choose a common surname for the duration of the union.

Italian Ministry of Justice (explanatory report on the decree implementing art. 1(28)(b) of Law 76/2016): describes treating same-sex marriages contracted abroad as producing the effects of a civil union under Italian law, and that a foreigner may form a civil union in Italy subject to the documentation rules.
facts.conflicts: Read via page summary only, not full text. Used to support 'Italy offers civil unions, not marriage, to same-sex couples'; confirm wording against Law 76/2016 and D.Lgs. 7/2017 before stating it as fact.

insider_details.detail: The Atto Notorio has a narrow window. Sydney's Italian consulate will not issue it more than six months before the wedding, Brisbane wants first contact at least a month before you fly, and Adelaide needs your details two weeks before the appointment. In practice the appointment sits between about six months and six weeks before departure, and the hard part is logistics, not paperwork: four adult witnesses who are not related to you (Brisbane adds 'known you for at least 12 months', Perth 'not sharing your surname') must all turn up in person with photo ID.

Order the paperwork in Australia in sequence: certificate from your state BDM, then the NAATI Italian translation, then DFAT apostilles. Sydney and Adelaide ask for apostilled translations as well as originals, and DFAT only legalises original Australian public documents, so a translation normally needs a Notary Public's notarisation before DFAT will apostille it. At A$105 per apostille (2026), two people with a birth certificate, single status certificate and translations each can mean eight apostilles, and DFAT warns of delays at the end of the school year and in holiday peaks.

Once in Italy, the order is Rome or Milan, then the Prefettura, then the comune, and offices keep weekday-morning hours (Rome's Prefettura legalisation office is open Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday, 9am to 12pm). Buy the EUR 16 marca da bollo at a tabaccaio before you queue. Some comuni want the sworn declaration at least three days before the ceremony even though the Embassy says it can be the same day, so build in a working week on the ground rather than flying in two days before.

For a May to September wedding, lock the comune slot first. The Embassy warns celebrant appointments and the post-wedding Apostille are hard to get in peak season, and a Tuscan comune such as Bagno a Ripoli asks for the date and room at least 90 days ahead, with witnesses named 15 days before. The interpreter is the couple's job, not the comune's.

Leave Italy with the apostilled marriage certificate in hand (ask for it at the Prefettura of the city where you married), because there is nothing to register at home. The marriage is recognised in Australia, but NSW and Victoria will not let you change surname on an overseas certificate, so the bride or groom taking a new name applies for a formal change of name through their state registry.

Same-sex couples: Italy's option is a civil union (unione civile) with two witnesses, and there are no multilingual extracts for civil unions. Australia recognises overseas same-sex marriages, but how it treats an Italian civil union is not confirmed by an Australian authority, so the clean route many couples take is to marry legally in Australia (Notice of Intended Marriage at least one month before) and hold the celebration in Italy. Your Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements with the comune.

open_questions.question: ANSWER to 'Add the Atto Notorio and Single Status Certificate to must_include?': yes. Every official source read (Embassy Rome PDF; Italian consulates Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide, Perth) requires the Atto Notorio, and Sydney and Adelaide also list an apostilled, translated Single Status Certificate (Brisbane: Letter of No Record for QLD, Letter of No Impediment for NT). Both are covered in must_include_coverage; the writer should treat them as must-includes.

ANSWERS to 02 verify_items: (1) Both partners attend the Atto Notorio appointment with 4 witnesses (Sydney, Brisbane); each Australian signs the Nulla Osta in person; appointment lead time at Rome/Milan is not published. (2) Witnesses: 4 at Italian consulates in Australia, 2 at a Tribunale in Italy; no official figure for the comune route (competitor claim of 4 unsupported). (3) Nulla Osta validity six months confirmed live; fee conflict A$80 / A$88 / A$90 (verify item 1). (4) Marca da bollo EUR 16 confirmed live. (5) Atto Notorio: Melbourne approx. AUD 45; Sydney EUR 28 / AUD 45.70 (Q4 2026 tariff, now read); Brisbane fee on review, cash only. (6) No national waiting period for non-residents: Embassy says same day is possible, two Tuscan comuni require 3 days; varies by comune. (7) Marriage Act Part VA s 88D read: recognised as valid subject to exceptions; Smartraveller and AGD wording confirmed. (8) Civil union: Law 76/2016 confirmed via Firenze; Australian treatment unresolved (verify items 3 to 5).

assumptions: Legal and document facts come only from government sources: Australian Embassy Rome, DFAT/Smartraveller, Attorney-General's Department, NSW and Victorian BDM registries, the Italian consulates in Australia (MAECI esteri.it sites) and Italian comune and ministry pages. Competitor and planner pages in 02-research/pages were used only to identify conflicts, never as sources.
Write every legal step with 'as at October 2026' and the line that your Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements (compliance-checklist.md; Embassy disclaimer fact_03).
The Marriage Act s 88D text was read on AustLII (source_type 'other'); link readers to the official legislation.gov.au series or to the AGD/Smartraveller pages rather than AustLII.

Comune pages from Bagno a Ripoli, Montespertoli, Firenze, Parma and Gossolengo are examples of comune practice, not national rules. The article should say 'for example' or 'some comuni' when using them.
Symbolic ceremony: no authority publishes a sentence saying a symbolic ceremony has no legal effect; it is phrased as plain advice that follows from the legal steps (facts 02, 28, 36).
